passage: Elizabeth read the message twice on the metro to college: a white van was taking children near schools, and it said forward to everyone you love. Her heart pounded. She sent it to the family group before the next station. By evening her aunt had phoned three neighbours and told the twin cousins not to walk to the park. Aparna, Elizabeth's cousin, texted privately: "Where did this come from? The photo looks old." Elizabeth's face went hot. She searched and found the same picture from another city years ago, with no local report at all. She deleted her forward, wrote "Sorry, I didn't check. Please ignore it," and phoned her aunt to explain.

qa.q: When did Elizabeth send the message to the family group?
qa.a: Elizabeth sent it before the next station.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth forward the message without checking?
qa.a: Fear made it feel urgent; the pounding heart and the line about forwarding to everyone loved made Elizabeth act at once.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do before forwarding a shocking message next time?
qa.a: Pause, check where it came from and whether any local report exists, and skip the forward if not.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's aunt have felt after phoning three neighbours?
qa.a: Worried, and then perhaps embarrassed once Elizabeth explained, because the panic had already spread.

grounding: A young adult forwards a shocking message to the family group unchecked, then learns to pause and check the source.

passage:
Kavitha: Damini, your Nani just phoned me in tears. She says the college is shutting for a week because of some threat.
Damini: Oh no. I forwarded that to the family group last night. It looked official.
Kavitha: Who wrote it?
Damini: I... it just said forward to everyone. No name.
Kavitha: Is there a notice on the college website?
Damini: Checking. Nothing. And the class group says lectures are normal.
Kavitha: So what now?
Damini: I'll delete it and write to the family, "That message was false, sorry, please ignore." And I'll ring Nani myself.
Kavitha: Good. Next time, check first.

qa.q: What did the message say would happen to the college?
qa.a: It said the college is shutting for a week because of some threat.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when forwarding the message to the family group?
qa.a: Damini was probably worried for the family, since the message looked official and important, so forwarding felt protective; Damini did not check who wrote it.

qa.q: What did Damini do to put things right?
qa.a: Checked the college website and class group, deleted the forward, told the family it was false and rang Nani.

qa.q: What is it like for Nani when a shocking false message arrives?
qa.a: Frightening; Nani was in tears on the phone before anyone knew whether it was true.

grounding: A young adult forwards a shocking message in a family group, then checks the source and corrects it.

passage: Shreya, before you press that forward button, let your Saurabh chacha tell you something. I was twenty, in Pune, and phones had just started sending messages to many people at once. One night a message came: the water supply in our area was poisoned, don't drink, forward to everyone. I felt a jolt, I tell you, like I was saving lives. I sent it to forty people. Our neighbour, old Mrs Kulkarni, who lived alone, didn't drink water for a whole day. She fainted on the stairs in the heat. It was all false. Someone made it up for fun. I sat with her at the clinic that evening and couldn't look at her. Next day I went to the municipal office and asked. That was the last time I forwarded anything without checking. You won't feel like a hero. That's alright.

qa.q: How many people did Saurabh send the message to?
qa.a: He sent it to forty people.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when he first read the message, and later at the clinic?
qa.a: At first he felt a jolt, as if he was saving lives; at the clinic he felt so ashamed he couldn't look at Mrs Kulkarni.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did young Saurabh change?
qa.a: Seeing Mrs Kulkarni faint because of the false message; after that he checked with the municipal office and stopped forwarding anything unchecked.

qa.q: How was Mrs Kulkarni affected by the rumour?
qa.a: Living alone, she believed it, went without water for a day and fainted on the stairs, so a made-up message caused her real harm.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who forwards a shocking message without checking, sees the harm it causes, and learns to pause and check the source.

passage:
Jomon's phone was on four per cent when the message landed in the family group: a blurry photo of a man near their colony gate, and the words "CHILD LIFTER SPOTTED, share urgently". His heart jumped. His little cousins played at that gate. With no time to think and the battery flashing, he forwarded it to three other groups, then the screen went black.
When he got to the hostel charger an hour later, there were forty messages. His cousin Mridul had written, "Jomon, this is Raju bhaiya who sells vegetables. People are shouting at him." Jomon felt sick. He called Mridul, who said a crowd had gathered, and the colony watchman had calmed them down.
Jomon posted in all four groups: "I forwarded without checking. This is false. The man is our vegetable seller. Please delete." Then he messaged Raju bhaiya's son to say sorry.

qa.q: What did the message in the family group claim?
qa.a: "CHILD LIFTER SPOTTED, share urgently", with a blurry photo of a man near the colony gate.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he read Mridul's message?
qa.a: Jomon felt sick with guilt and shock, realising the forward had put an innocent man in danger.

qa.q: How did Jomon try to repair the harm, and what could he do next time?
qa.a: He posted a clear correction in every group and apologised to the seller's son; next time he could pause, especially under pressure, and check before forwarding.

qa.q: What is it like for Raju bhaiya when the message spreads?
qa.a: He is suddenly treated as a criminal by people who buy from him, frightened by a shouting crowd over a photo he never knew was taken.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who forwards a shocking message without checking, sees it harm an innocent man, and corrects it.

passage:
Rekha was halfway through her lunch at the Hyderabad office canteen when the family group lit up. A message with the municipal logo: the tap water in their ward was contaminated, don't drink, stock up on cans. Nani had already replied with three praying hands. Rekha's thumb hovered over forward. Her aunt's family lived in the next ward, with a newborn.
"What's that face?" asked Gurleen, sitting opposite.
Rekha showed her. Gurleen frowned. "The logo's stretched. And 'contaminated' is spelled wrong."
Rekha opened the municipal website. No notice. She searched the ward name. Nothing. She felt a strange mix of relief and embarrassment. She typed in the family group instead: "I checked, there's no notice from the corporation. Please don't forward, it looks fake." Nani wrote back, "Oh! Thank you, beta." Rekha finished her cold rice, a bit slower.

qa.q: What did Gurleen notice about the message?
qa.a: The logo was stretched and "contaminated" was spelled wrong.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling after she found no notice on the website?
qa.a: She felt a mix of relief and embarrassment, relieved it was false and a little embarrassed she nearly forwarded it.

qa.q: What small steps helped Rekha avoid spreading the rumour?
qa.a: Pausing before forwarding, looking closely with a friend, and checking the official website for a notice before posting a calm correction.

qa.q: How might Nani have been affected if Rekha had forwarded the message?
qa.a: Nani, who already reacted with worry, might have panicked more and spread it further; the correction instead brought her relief.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult about to forward a shocking message, who pauses, checks the source and skips the forward.

passage:
"Payal, did you forward this to the family group?" Kamal held up his phone: "Kidnappers in white vans taking children from school gates in our city."
"Yes! Bua's kids walk to school. People need to know."
"Where did it come from?"
"Mausi's friend sent it. It had a photo and everything."
"Look at the photo. That bus stop sign is in another language. And the city police page says there's no such case."
Payal's face went warm. "But it felt so important."
"That's how they're written. Chachi has already kept Anu home from school. Nani's crying."
"Oh no." Payal typed fast in the group: "Please ignore my last forward. I didn't check it. The police say it isn't true. Sorry, everyone."
"Good," Kamal said. "Next time, pause first. If you can't find where it came from, don't send it."

qa.q: Who had kept Anu home from school?
qa.a: Chachi had kept Anu home from school.

qa.q: Why did Payal forward the message in the first place?
qa.a: Payal was worried about Bua's kids and believed it was important, so fear pushed her to share without checking.

qa.q: What did Payal get right once she learnt the truth?
qa.a: She quickly posted a correction in the group, admitted she hadn't checked, pointed to the police and apologised.

qa.q: How might Nani have experienced the forward?
qa.a: Nani was frightened for the grandchildren and ended up crying, which shows how an unchecked rumour hurts real people.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who forwards a shocking message in a family group without checking, sees the harm, and learns to pause and check the source.
